description: Who business stakeholders are and how their interests can clash.
content_html:
Who Are Stakeholders?

A stakeholder is anyone who has an interest in a business — whether they work for it, own it, buy from it, live near it, or campaign around it. This is broader than a shareholder, who is just one type of stakeholder. A shareholder owns part of the business; a stakeholder might simply live on the street behind the factory.

Businesses do not exist in isolation. Every decision — where to locate, how many staff to employ, what to charge — affects people beyond the owners. Understanding who those people are, and what they want, is essential for running a sustainable business.

Key Fact

The eight stakeholder groups are: shareholders (owners), employees, customers, managers, suppliers, local community, pressure groups and the government. Each has different objectives, and those objectives frequently conflict.

The Eight Stakeholder Groups

Shareholders own the business. Their primary objective is a return on their investment — they want the business to make profit so they can receive dividends and see the value of their shares rise. For a sole trader or partnership, the owner is the main decision-maker as well as the stakeholder most exposed to financial risk.

Employees want good pay, job security, safe working conditions and opportunities for career development. Their wellbeing depends directly on how the business performs and on the employment decisions managers make.

Customers want good-quality products at fair prices, with reliable service and legal protection if things go wrong. Without customers spending money, the business cannot survive.

Managers run the day-to-day operations. They may be shareholders in a large company, but in a small business the manager is often also the founder. Managers typically want the business to grow, which increases their own status, salary and decision-making power.

Suppliers sell goods or services to the business. They want prompt payment, long-term contracts and fair prices. A reliable business customer helps a supplier plan its own production and cash flow.

The local community is affected by a business through employment, traffic, noise, pollution and investment in local infrastructure. A new distribution centre might bring 200 jobs but also lorry movements at 3 am — residents experience both sides.

Pressure groups campaign on specific issues — environmental groups, animal rights organisations or trade unions fall into this category. They can influence consumer behaviour, attract media attention and lobby government for tighter regulation. A well-organised campaign can change a business’s practices even without legal compulsion.

The government wants businesses to operate lawfully, pay taxes, provide employment and contribute to economic growth. It shapes the environment through taxation, regulation and public spending decisions. For a small business, changes in the minimum wage, tax rates or planning rules can have an immediate impact on costs and plans.

How Stakeholders Affect and Are Affected by Business

Influence flows in both directions. Businesses affect stakeholders through the decisions they make: cutting staff affects employees; moving production overseas affects suppliers; raising prices affects customers. But stakeholders also shape business decisions: a customer boycott can reverse a policy; a trade union can negotiate better pay; a pressure group campaign can force a business to adopt environmental standards it would otherwise have ignored.

Small businesses often feel stakeholder pressure most acutely because they have less financial cushion. A single large customer withdrawing their contract, or a negative review on social media going viral, can threaten a small firm’s survival in a way that a large corporation might survive easily.

Key Fact

Stakeholder conflict arises when two groups want different outcomes from the same business decision. The most common conflict is between shareholders (who want maximum profit) and employees (who want higher wages — which reduce profit). High marks on extended-response questions require you to show how the interests collide, not just list them separately.

Common Stakeholder Conflicts

Conflict between shareholders and employees is the most frequently examined. Shareholders want to maximise profit; employees want higher wages and better conditions. These objectives pull in opposite directions because wages are a cost that reduces profit.

Customers and shareholders can also conflict. Customers want the lowest possible price; shareholders want the highest possible profit margin. A business that cuts prices to win customers may satisfy one group while disappointing the other.

The local community often conflicts with businesses over expansion. A supermarket opening a new store brings jobs but can destroy footfall for independent local shops — some residents welcome it, others campaign against it. These competing views both count as stakeholder responses to the same decision.

Shareholders and managers can also conflict, particularly in larger companies. Shareholders want short-term profit and dividends; managers may want to reinvest profit into growth that benefits them in the long run but reduces the immediate dividend payout. This is called the principal–agent problem in business theory, though at GCSE level the focus stays on naming the conflict and explaining its consequences.

The government may conflict with businesses when it introduces new regulations or raises the minimum wage. Businesses see this as a cost increase; the government sees it as protecting workers. Both positions are driven by legitimate stakeholder interests.

Managing Stakeholder Conflict

Businesses manage stakeholder conflict through compromise. A firm might increase wages by a smaller amount than employees demand but more than shareholders initially wanted. It might consult the local community before submitting a planning application, adjusting its design to reduce noise or traffic impact. These are not perfect solutions for any single group, but they are the practical reality of running a business inside a complex web of competing interests.

For your exam answers, the key is to show the conflict explicitly — name the two groups, state what each wants, explain why those objectives collide, and then assess the impact on the business. An answer that describes each group’s interests separately without showing the collision will not reach the upper tiers of the mark scheme.
exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark Explain question about stakeholders, you only need two well-developed points — do not rush into a third or fourth. Each point should state what a stakeholder group wants, then develop with two linked expansion sentences explaining why that objective creates tension or affects the business. No case-study context is needed on Explain questions. For a 9-mark Analyse in Context response, embed specific details from the scenario — the business name alone earns nothing; you must use the product, location or financial figures given. The most common error on stakeholder questions is listing groups in parallel without ever showing how their interests directly collide — examiners reward the collision, not the list.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are eight stakeholder groups — shareholders, employees, customers, managers, suppliers, local community, pressure groups and the government — each with different objectives.
  • Stakeholders both affect and are affected by business decisions; influence flows in both directions, and small businesses are especially vulnerable to stakeholder pressure.
  • Stakeholder conflict arises when groups want opposite outcomes from the same decision; high-mark answers show the collision explicitly rather than listing interests separately.

practice_questions.marks: Any individual or group with an interest in a business who is affected by, or can affect, its decisions. [1 mark — must distinguish from shareholder; accept: 'any person or group with an interest in a business']

practice_questions.text: Outline two objectives of employees as stakeholders in a business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each objective identified (up to 2) and 1 further mark for developing one of them with a linked explanation.

Acceptable objectives: good pay / fair wages; job security; safe working conditions; career progression / training opportunities; good working conditions.

Example developed point: Employees want job security [1] because losing their job means losing income, which affects their ability to pay bills and support their family [1]. [3 marks total: 1 + 1 + 1]

practice_questions.text:
Priya runs a small bakery called Clover & Crumb in Harrogate. She has five full-time employees. Her landlord has just raised the rent by £400 per month. Priya is considering cutting one member of staff to cover the extra cost.

Explain how this decision could conflict with the interests of two different stakeholder groups.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two well-developed points, each identifying a stakeholder group, stating their objective and explaining clearly why the decision conflicts with it. Both points fully developed with two logical expansion sentences.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two points identified with at least one developed explanation. Some link to conflict made, though one point may lack a second expansion.

Developing (2 marks): One or two stakeholder groups named with a basic statement of conflict but limited development.

Emerging (1 mark): A stakeholder group is named but no explanation of conflict is given.

Example content:
• Employees want job security — cutting a member of staff means one person loses their income and may face financial hardship. Remaining employees may also feel less secure, reducing morale and productivity. [developed]
• Customers want consistent, reliable service — with one fewer member of staff, the bakery may be slower at peak times, reducing service quality and risking customer loss to competitors. [developed]

practice_questions.text:
Clover & Crumb bakery has been trading for three years in Harrogate. It has built a loyal customer base, but a national bakery chain is planning to open nearby. Priya’s five employees are worried about job security. Local residents have mixed views: some welcome the choice; others support the independent business.

Analyse how stakeholder conflict might affect Priya’s decision-making at Clover & Crumb.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Develops two or more stakeholder conflicts in context, using specific scenario details (employees, local residents, the new competitor, Priya as owner). Analyses how conflicting pressures shape the decision and reaches a reasoned conclusion about the impact on the business. Embeds contextual details throughout, not just in the opening sentence.

Secure (5–7 marks): At least two stakeholder conflicts identified and linked to the scenario. Context used at least once per point but may not be fully embedded. Analysis present but may not fully extend to consequences for decision-making.

Developing (3–4 marks): Some reference to stakeholder conflict and some use of scenario details, but explanation is limited or conflict is described without analysis of the decision-making impact.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names stakeholders or identifies a conflict but makes little use of the scenario and provides minimal analysis.

Example content points:
• Conflict between Priya (shareholder objective: protect profit) and employees (job security): if Priya cuts staff to reduce costs, employees lose income; if she does not cut staff but profit falls due to competition, she risks the business’s survival, which ultimately threatens all employees anyway.
• Conflict between local community supporters (who want the independent bakery to survive) and customers who prefer the lower prices a chain may offer: Priya must decide whether to compete on price or differentiate on quality and local identity.
• Conflict with the local community: residents supporting Clover & Crumb place pressure on Priya to stay open and maintain her offer, but if footfall falls she may need to change hours or reduce the product range.

practice_questions.text:
'Shareholders are always the most important stakeholder group for any business.'

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A balanced evaluation that develops arguments both supporting and challenging the statement, embeds business knowledge throughout, and reaches a justified conclusion that goes beyond simply restating prior points. The conclusion identifies specific conditions under which the statement holds or does not hold.

Secure (7–9 marks): Arguments on both sides with some development. Knowledge of stakeholder theory accurate. Conclusion present and justified, though may be brief or slightly formulaic.

Developing (4–6 marks): Some arguments on one or both sides. Limited development or a conclusion that only restates the arguments without adding evaluative judgement.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points about shareholders or other stakeholders, with little evaluation and no reasoned conclusion.

Arguments supporting the statement:
• Shareholders bear the financial risk — without their investment, the business cannot start or grow. Satisfying shareholders ensures the business has access to further capital.
• Profit, which flows to shareholders, is the measure most business decisions are ultimately judged by; without profit, the business cannot pay employees, suppliers or the government.
• In a start-up or small sole-trader business, the owner (shareholder) makes every decision, so their objectives automatically drive the business.

Arguments against the statement:
• Customers are arguably more important to survival: without revenue from customers, there is no profit to distribute to shareholders. A business that ignores customer needs will fail regardless of shareholder wishes.
• Employees deliver the product or service — a business that treats staff badly faces high turnover, low productivity and reputational damage that ultimately harms shareholder returns.
• Government and legislation cannot be ignored: a business that breaks employment law or consumer law faces fines, closure or reputational damage that destroys shareholder value entirely.
• For a social enterprise or co-operative, the community or employees may be the primary stakeholder by design.

Conclusion should recognise that the relative importance of stakeholders depends on the type of business, its stage of development, and the specific decision being taken — for a profit-maximising plc shareholders may dominate, but for a small independent business, customers and the local community may be equally or more important to daily survival.

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which a pressure group can affect a small business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each valid way, up to 2.

Acceptable answers: organise a consumer boycott / campaign on social media to damage the business’s reputation / lobby government to change legislation affecting the business / stage protests outside the business / publish negative media stories about the business’s practices. [2 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes a stakeholder?
options: Someone who owns shares in a limited company
Any individual or group with an interest in a business
An employee who has worked at a business for more than one year
A government official who inspects business premises

knowledge_checks.q: Which stakeholder conflict is most commonly examined in Business GCSE questions?
A _____ is an organised group that campaigns to change business or government behaviour on a specific issue.
Shareholders want maximum profit, while employees want higher wages — this creates a stakeholder _____ because the two objectives pull in opposite directions.
Match each stakeholder to their primary objective:
right: Maximum profit and return on investment
Good quality products at fair prices

flashcard_questions.a: Any individual or group with an interest in a business, affected by or able to affect its decisions.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a stakeholder differ from a shareholder?
flashcard_questions.a: A shareholder is one type of stakeholder — an owner of shares. Stakeholders include everyone affected by the business.

flashcard_questions.q: What do shareholders primarily want from a business?
flashcard_questions.a: Profit and a return on their investment, through dividends or rising share value.

flashcard_questions.q: What do employees want from a business?
flashcard_questions.a: Good pay, job security, safe working conditions and opportunities for career development.

flashcard_questions.q: What do suppliers want from the businesses they supply?
flashcard_questions.a: Prompt payment, fair prices and long-term contracts.
An organised group that campaigns to change business or government behaviour on a specific issue.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do shareholders and employees often have conflicting objectives?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher wages reduce profit; shareholders want maximum profit, so their interests pull in opposite directions.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one way a pressure group can affect a small business.
flashcard_questions.a: By organising a consumer boycott or using social media to damage the business's reputation.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the government want from businesses operating in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: Lawful operation, tax payment, job creation and contribution to economic growth.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are customers considered essential stakeholders for any business?
flashcard_questions.a: Without customer spending, the business earns no revenue and cannot survive.

flashcard_questions.q: How can a business manage stakeholder conflict?
flashcard_questions.a: Through compromise — for example, raising wages by less than demanded but more than shareholders initially wanted.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is simply listing stakeholder interests not enough in an extended-response answer?
flashcard_questions.a: Examiners reward answers that show how interests collide, not just describe each group separately.

glossary_terms.definition: Any individual or group with an interest in a business and who is affected by, or can affect, its decisions.
An owner of shares in a company who has invested capital and receives a dividend if profits are distributed.
An organised group that campaigns to change business or government behaviour on a specific issue, such as the environment or animal welfare.
The conflict that arises when an agent (manager) makes decisions on behalf of a principal (shareholder) but does not always act in the principal's best interest.
A share of a company's profits paid out to shareholders as a return on their investment.
A situation where two or more stakeholder groups want different outcomes from the same business decision, pulling in opposite directions.
